desc:
Return the n-th smallest positive integer that is divisible by at least one of a, b and c.

Example: for n = 5, a = 2, b = 3, c = 5 the qualifying numbers are 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, ..., so the answer is 6.

The test data guarantees that the answer does not exceed 2 * 109.
hints: Counting by stepping through integers is far too slow. Count how many qualifying integers are at most a given x instead.
Adding x // a + x // b + x // c counts numbers divisible by two of the values twice (or three times). Fix it with inclusion-exclusion using least common multiples.
count(x) = x//a + x//b + x//c - x//lcm(a,b) - x//lcm(b,c) - x//lcm(a,c) + x//lcm(a,b,c). It is non-decreasing; binary search the smallest x in [1, 2*109] with count(x) ≥ n.
editorial: The inclusion-exclusion principle gives the number of integers in 1..x divisible by at least one of the three values: add single multiples, subtract pairwise-lcm multiples, add the multiples of the lcm of all three. All least common multiples are computed once with lcm(u, v) = u / gcd(u, v) * v. They can be as large as 1027; in languages with 64-bit integers cap them at something above the search limit (e.g. 2·109 + 1), since a divisor larger than x contributes zero.

The count is non-decreasing in x and increments exactly at qualifying numbers. The smallest x with count(x) ≥ n is therefore the answer, and the statement guarantees x ≤ 2·109, so the search range is [1, 2·109] (about 31 iterations).
Time O(log 2·10<sup>9</sup>) with a constant number of gcd computations, space O(1). The same idea extends to any number of divisors (with subsets), just with more terms.
